query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The degradation of the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA at elevated temperatures is governed by the formation (or lack thereof) of a continuous, grain-boundary‐assisted Al2O3 inner scale that protects the nanocrystalline fcc matrix. In oxidizing environments, rapid outward diffusion of Al along the high-density grain boundaries promotes a thin, adherent Al2O3 layer that preserves mechanical integrity, whereas under reducing conditions a less continuous oxide forms and localized Al depletion at grain boundaries leads to internal oxidation and microstructural degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured, nanocrystalline fcc Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy with a high density of grain boundaries and balanced elemental distribution designed for high strength and fatigue performance.
generation.intervention: Expose specimens to controlled high-temperature aging regimes in either an oxidizing (air or O2-rich) or reducing (H2 or inert gas) gas environment.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperatures ranging between approximately 800 °C and 1200 °C with well-controlled oxidizing versus reducing gas atmospheres.
generation.structural_mediator: The nanocrystalline microstructure and its abundant grain boundaries which serve as fast diffusion pathways for Al.
generation.mechanism: In oxidizing gas environments, high-temperature exposure accelerates Al diffusion along grain boundaries, leading to the rapid formation of a continuous Al2O3 inner oxide scale that adheres well to the substrate and limits further oxidation. In contrast, in reducing conditions the slower or incomplete oxidation of Al leads to local depletion near grain boundaries, resulting in internal oxidation and microstructural damage that diminishes ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under oxidizing conditions, microstructural analyses (e.g., TEM/EDS) will reveal a thin, continuous and adherent Al2O3 inner layer with minimal evidence of internal oxidation, thereby preserving the alloy’s mechanical integrity. Under reducing environments, the oxide scale will be discontinuous or thicker with evidence of localized internal oxidation along grain boundaries, correlating with early signs of embrittlement or reduced fatigue performance.
generation.baseline: The as-built HEA exhibits a nanocrystalline fcc matrix with high strength and fatigue resistance, with no pre-existing oxide scale.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be active for exposures at temperatures between ~800 °C and 1200 °C; effects may deviate outside this range or under rapid thermal cycling conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The precise rate of Al diffusion and the extent of oxide scale anchoring under varying gas compositions have not been fully quantified, and subtle synergistic effects of other elements (e.g., Cr and Ti) in modifying scale adhesion require further clarification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare multiple sample sets of the HEA and subject them to identical high-temperature aging protocols in either oxidizing or reducing gas environments at temperatures within the 800 °C to 1200 °C range. After exposure, use high-resolution TEM combined with EDS to characterize the continuity, thickness, and composition of oxide scales, particularly the presence and distribution of Al2O3. Additionally, assess mechanical performance (e.g., fatigue and tensile properties) and correlate these findings with the microstructural analyses.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and continuity via TEM/EDS
Grain boundary composition and evidence of internal oxidation
Mechanical test results (strength, ductility, fatigue life) post-exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If oxidizing environment samples do not exhibit a continuous, adherent Al2O3 inner layer (or show similar internal oxidation and mechanical degradation as reducing environment samples), then the hypothesis that grain-boundary-assisted Al diffusion is the primary mechanism governing degradation is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Among the various HEA systems, FeNiCuAl-based alloys are of particular interest because they combine relatively low raw-material cost with favorable overall performance. However, their insufficient oxidation resistance at temperatures of 900 °C and above remains a major obstacle to practical high-temperature applications [,,]. During oxidation, alloy durability is largely determined by the composition, compactness, adhesion, and growth kinetics of the surface oxide scale [,,]. In particular, the formation of a dense, continuous, and strongly adherent protective scale is essential for suppressing inward oxygen diffusion and outward metal-cation transport, thereby slowing oxidation and preventing premature scale failure [,,]. Alloying is an effective approach for improving the oxidation resistance of FeNiCuAl-based HEAs [,,]. Cr and Al are well known to promote the formation of thermodynamically stable Cr2O3 and Al2O3 protective scales, respectively, whereas Co can facilitate spinel formation and Mn can promote the development of MnCr2O4 while improving scale integrity and adhesion [,,]. Based on the comprehensive experimental observations and kinetic analysis, the superior high-temperature oxidation mechanism of the Innovation Alloy is schematically summarized in Figure 8. The laser-cladding-induced nanocrystalline structure provides a high density of grain boundaries, which act as short-circuit diffusion pathways, promoting the rapid formation of a continuous and protective Al2O3 inner layer. The synergistic addition of Cr and Mn facilitates the development of a stable MnCr2O4/Cr2O3 outer layer. Furthermore, the reactive element Y segregates at the scale/alloy interface as fine Y2O3 particles, which effectively anchor the oxide scale through a pinning effect, thereby preventing spallation and ensuring long-term protection at high temperatures. This multi-level synergistic effect leads to the exceptional oxidation resistance of the Innovation Alloy compared to the Base and Synergy Alloys.
